title-group.article-title: Chronic negative-pressure hydrocephalus: management of prolonged subatmospheric drainage failure and treatment approach in persistent ventriculomegaly. Illustrative case

sec.title: BACKGROUND
sec.p: Chronic negative-pressure hydrocephalus (cNegPH) is a rare condition, with only a few cases reported worldwide. Improvement of symptoms correlates with a reduction in ventricular size, which has been well documented in low-pressure hydrocephalus after prolonged subatmospheric cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) drainage and is considered the standard of care in such cases. However, the management of treatment failure and manifestation of cNegPH is still challenging, as well-documented treatment concepts are lacking.

sec.title: OBSERVATIONS
sec.p: Ventriculomegaly in a 36-year-old posthemorrhage, posttrauma patient with hydrocephalus remained refractory to low-gradient ventriculoperitoneal shunting, neck wrapping, endoscopic third ventriculostomy, and prolonged subatmospheric CSF drainage. Extended clinical care with multiple surgical and diagnostic interventions such as repeated replacements of the external ventricular drainage catheter, ventriculoperitoneal shunt revisions, and multiple cranial computed tomography scans was required in the course of the diagnosis. Complications including shunt malfunction, infection, meningitis, and recurrent clinical deteriorations were observed.

sec.title: LESSONS
sec.p: Diagnosing cNegPH can be challenging, and the failure of common treatment approaches has to be accepted after a certain point in time. At such a point, alternative options must be considered to provide outpatient care and reduce the risk of treatment complications. Intermittent shunt reservoir pressing proved to be an adequate long-term treatment option with a favorable outcome at the 6-month follow-up.

body.p: Hydrocephalus is one of the major complications in severe posttraumatic brain injury with an unfavorable clinical prognosis.1 The standard procedure for treatment involves the use of ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) systems that can be customized to meet the individual needs of patients based on their age and health status. Today, programmable VPS valves are available that can be externally adjusted to achieve the desired pressure gradient and flow rate, ensuring effective management of VPS under- or overdrainage.

Low-pressure hydrocephalus (LPH) and negative-pressure hydrocephalus (NegPH) are rare types of hydrocephalus characterized by either low or negative intraventricular pressure (IVP) and ventriculomegaly, accompanied by clinical signs of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), including headache, vomiting, and deterioration of consciousness. Patients with LPH or NegPH often undergo multiple shunt revisions without ventriculomegaly being successfully treated.

Although the pathophysiology of this condition is not yet fully understood, the neurological impairment is thought to be related to ventricle size rather than IVP. The literature indicates that the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms include alterations in the permeability and viscoelasticity of the brain tissue,2 as well as an imbalance of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation within the craniospinal subarachnoid space. Pang and Altschuler reported that scaled subatmospheric CSF drainage restores brain viscoelasticity, leading to a normalized ventricular pressure state.2 This treatment remains the most commonly used method, which can be titrated up to the pressure gradient at which VPS systems with low opening pressure can theoretically be applied. Other treatment options such as neck wrapping,3 endoscopic ventriculostomy of the third ventricle,4 and lumbar blood patches have also been described.3

Various terms have been used to describe persistent ventriculomegaly during CSF drainage therapy, such as “refractory LPH”5 and “syndrome of inappropriately low-pressure acute hydrocephalus.”6 However, these factors are inadequate for categorizing an evolving condition.

Wu et al. proposed a new classification of hydrocephalus based on ICP in the ventricular system. This classification includes high-pressure hydrocephalus, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, LPH, and NegPH.7 The inclusion of the terms “acute” and “chronic” in this classification could provide a more comprehensive description of the clinical presentation. Nevertheless, the precise point at which chronicity will manifest remains uncertain, and the efficacy of conventional therapeutic modalities may be limited. Consequently, the diagnosis and treatment of these conditions can still be fraught with difficulty. This report discusses common treatment failure and proposes an alternative approach for a 36-year-old female with NegPH that did not respond to low-gradient ventriculoperitoneal shunting, neck wrapping, endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV), and prolonged subatmospheric CSF drainage and was therefore considered chronic. As suggested by Kalani et al.,5 intermittent shunt reservoir pressing (iSRP) was evaluated for functionality, CSF drainage, and outpatient management.

sec.title: Patient Synopsis
sec.p:
A 36-year-old female experienced a severe traumatic brain injury, including a left hemispheric acute subdural hematoma (aSDH) and traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (Fig. 1A). Because of a sudden deterioration in consciousness and progression of the aSDH, the patient underwent hemicraniectomy (Fig. 1B). After receiving complex intensive medical therapy and a rehabilitation interval, the patient developed posttraumatic hydrocephalus (Fig. 1C) and was treated with the implantation of a VPS (proGAV valve, Christoph Miethke GmbH & Co. KG). Subsequently, while experiencing sinking flap syndrome, cranioplasty was performed 3 months after the initial trauma (Fig. 1D and E). After postoperative care without complications, the patient was discharged a few days later. FIG. 1.
Cranial CT scans of the initial trauma (A), after left hemicraniectomy (B), demonstrating acute normal-pressure hydrocephalus (C), demonstrating sinking flap syndrome (D), after cranioplasty (E), and after the development of LPH (F). Cranial MRI of ventriculomegaly with PVL (G), and cranial CT scan of persistent ventriculomegaly after EVD placement (H).

However, in the subsequent period, the patient experienced repeated deterioration of consciousness as a result of recurrent ventriculomegaly, requiring multiple valve adjustments and short clinical admittances. Finally, shunt malfunction was suspected. The patient was readmitted for VPS revision and implantation of an M.blue plus valve system (Christoph Miethke GmbH & Co. KG), which consists of an adjustable differential pressure unit (proGav 2.0) and an adjustable gravitational unit (M.blue) and was initially set to 18/4 cm H2O. The procedure was performed without complications, and the patient was discharged again. Shortly afterward, the patient presented to the emergency department with reduced consciousness, as evidenced by a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8. In addition, anisocoria was detected, with the right pupil noticeably larger than the left.

A subsequent cranial computed tomography (CT) scan revealed recurrent ventricular enlargement (Fig. 1F). Immediately, 50 ml of CSF was aspirated through the reservoir, and the shunt valve was adjusted to a lower pressure level of 10/3 cm H2O. Shunt series radiographs showed an intact shunt system without kinking or discontinuity, and the modified valve setting was confirmed. Subsequently, the patient’s consciousness improved to a GCS score of 11. After a renewed deterioration in consciousness just a few hours later, an additional 40 ml of CSF was withdrawn via the reservoir, which again resulted in a positive clinical response. The shunt valve was finally set to a position of 0/0 cm H2O, avoiding any further valve resistance. Follow-up cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no competing cause for the clinical deterioration but did show further enlargement of the ventricles with periventricular lucency (PVL; Fig. 1G). The chemical analysis of the CSF yielded no abnormal results. Although the patient was more alert, she still showed severe psychomotor impairment with no speech production or spontaneous movement. Under the clinical assumption of LPH, the ventricular catheter was removed, the VPS was ligated, and an external ventricular drain (EVD) was placed in the right lateral ventricle for external CSF drainage. However, it was not possible to drain a sufficient amount of CSF when the EVD was positioned at an atmospheric pressure level ≥ 0 cm H2O, so ventriculomegaly initially persisted after EVD placement (Fig. 1H).

sec.title: Subatmospheric CSF Drainage and ETV
sec.p:
As a result, subatmospheric CSF drainage was performed via the EVD, starting at a level of −10 cm below the external auditory canal (EAC) with a drainage rate of 5–15 ml/hr. The efficacy of drainage was determined clinically by monitoring the patient’s consciousness, speech production, and vegetative symptoms such as nausea and vomiting. In addition, it was ensured that an adequate amount of CSF was drained per day, and serial cranial CT scans were obtained to assess changes in ventricle size. The original treatment strategy was to achieve EVD weaning by raising the draining chamber by 2 cm at 3-day intervals when the clinical parameters were stable. In the event of clinical deterioration, correlating with radiographically confirmed ventricular CSF accumulation, the drainage chamber was lowered again. As shown in Fig. 2, multiple attempts were made with recurring ventriculomegaly (Fig. 3A–E). Assuming a refractory therapeutic strategy, ETV was performed as proposed by Hamilton and Price.6 The permeability of the ETV was confirmed intraoperatively through observation of pulsatile CSF flow through the defect. However, a positive flow void signal could not be detected over the floor of the third ventricle on postoperative MRI (Fig. 3F), thus not definitively confirming permeability. It is noteworthy that thickening of the subarachnoid septa was also observed during the procedure, suggesting inflammatory changes within the subarachnoid space, which could have resulted in the obstruction of CSF flow over the ETV. Given these findings, a subsequent intervention was not attempted. Over a period of 4 days, the patient again experienced loss of speech, followed by a decline in GCS score. Ventricular CSF accumulation was confirmed by cranial CT scanning, indicating that the ETV procedure had evidently failed, so the patient was treated with external ventricular drainage again, draining at subatmospheric levels. After an already prolonged clinical stay, the interval in which the draining chamber was raised was extended to 7 days. However, this approach did not lead to successful weaning from the EVD to a pressure level that would have allowed placement of a definitive low-pressure VPS (Fig. 3G). Given the final diagnosis of chronic negative-pressure hydrocephalus (cNegPH) with a necessary drainage level of −6 cm below the EAC, an alternative strategy for further outpatient management had to be considered. FIG. 2.
The course of subatmospheric CSF drainage over a treatment period of 180 days in correlation with ventricle size. FIG. 3.
Cranial CT scans of refractory subatmospheric CSF drainage (A–E), sagittal cranial T2-weighted MRI without a flow void sign over the floor of the third ventricle (F), and cranial CT scan of persistent ventriculomegaly after ETV (G).

sec.title: Shunt System
sec.p:
Currently, no VPS system available can independently establish a negative ventricular outflow gradient. The only way to generate negative pressure for CSF flow via a closed implanted system is through active iSRP. For this purpose, an M.blue plus VPS system was implanted, with a single catheter placed in the right lateral ventricle through Kocher’s point. Ventricular isolation was ruled out prior to the procedure. A control reservoir with a recoil mechanism was placed proximal to the shunt valves to prevent CSF from flowing back into the ventricle when the reservoir was pressed upon (Fig. 4 E– G). To confirm the functionality of iSRP, 2 ml of contrast medium was injected into the control reservoir, and the reservoir was then manually depressed to pump CSF. Subsequent CT scans of the cranium and abdomen showed unidirectional accumulation of contrast agent intraperitoneally but no intracranial reflux. The reservoir was tunneled temporally between the skin incisions to prevent pain and wound-healing disorders caused by repeated depression of the reservoir during iSRP. The shunt valves were placed retroauricularly and set to 0/0 cm H2O (Fig. 4). FIG. 4.
Left:Three-dimensional skull reconstruction after implantation of the M.blue plus VPS system with the borehole above Kocher’s point (A), temporally tunneled control reservoir (B), and retroauricularly positioned proGav 2.0 (C) and M.blue valve (D). Right:Schematic of the Miethke control reservoir in its resting position (E), its compressed position with 0.25 ml unidirectional CSF outflow (F), and its expanding position with 0.25 ml unidirectional CSF inflow (G). Original illustration: Christoph Miethke GmbH & Co. KG, www.miethke.com.

sec.title: Intermittent Shunt Reservoir Pressing
sec.p:
According to the manufacturer, each depression of the control reservoir pumps 0.25 ml of CSF. During EVD treatment with subatmospheric pressure, an average drainage of 160 ml CSF per day was needed to maintain a stable ventricle size. To further normalize the ventricle size, 180 ml CSF per day was initially drained through active iSRP. After a short monitoring period, overdrainage was observed on follow-up cranial CT (Fig. 5B). Therefore, manual iSRP was reduced to 4 cycles of 160 depressions per day, draining 40 ml each cycle. As a result, the patient experienced headaches toward the end of each cycle, which is why the interval was changed to 6 cycles of 107 pump strokes, draining 26.7 ml each time. Under these conditions, an appropriate ventricle size could be established and maintained, and the patient’s clinical condition stabilized. The patient’s husband was trained to perform iSRP to provide outpatient care. After a subsequent observational period, the patient was discharged and closely monitored through weekly follow-up appointments. Following a 6-month outpatient follow-up period, the patient demonstrated full recovery of her strength and ability to speak and was able to resume her daily activities. There was no further loss of consciousness and no further episodes of loss of speech. On occasion, iSRP was accompanied by episodes of headaches that lasted between 5 and 10 minutes. Compressions were then discontinued for that cycle. A final cranial CT scan demonstrated a slight increase in ventricle size, particularly in the left hemisphere, with the ventricular catheter positioned on the right side (Fig. 5D). Given the patient’s favorable clinical status, it was assumed that adequate CSF drainage was, however, maintained through iSRP. FIG. 5.
Cranial CT scans before (A) and during (B and C) clinical adjustment and after 6 months of iSRP (D).

sec.title: Complications
sec.p: As a consequence of prolonged intensive care treatment with frequent catheter changes, recurrent episodes of clinical deterioration, and the patient’s preexisting health conditions, a number of adverse events occurred, complicating medical treatment and prolonging the hospital stay. The patient had diabetes mellitus type 1 and subsequent terminal kidney failure with the need for 3 cycles of hemodialysis per week prior to the initial trauma. Further preconditions included diabetic retinopathy, diabetic polyneuropathy, coronary heart disease with acute myocardial infarction, hyperthyroidism as a result of Basedow’s disease, and arterial hypertension.

Because of sudden changes in consciousness and recurring malnutrition, the patient experienced periods of both hypo- and hyperglycemic states, which were in turn accompanied by clinical deterioration.

A series of EVD changes was performed at regular intervals of 4 weeks for the purpose of infection prophylaxis. However, as a consequence of prolonged EVD treatment, the patient developed meningitis and ventriculitis due to a catheter-associated infection with Staphylococcus epidermidis. Consequently, the previously temporarily ligated VPS system was removed, and the patient underwent a period of antibiotic treatment prior to VPS reimplantation. Further complications included hospital-acquired pneumonia and cholecystectomy following an episode of acute acalculous cholecystitis. In addition, intermittent stress reactions and psychosocial influences associated with prolonged intensive care unit treatment were observed.

sec.title: Informed Consent
sec.p: The necessary informed consent was obtained in this study.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This case report illustrates the complexity of this rare form of hydrocephalus, highlights challenges and complications, and provides a well-documented treatment plan to guide the management of patients with cNegPH whose conditions are refractory to subatmospheric CSF drainage. Treatment inevitably requires extended periods of intensive care, which can be associated with both medical and sociopsychological challenges for the patient. It is therefore imperative to accept the failure of common treatment after a certain point and consider alternative options to ensure outpatient care and reduce the risk of treatment complications and unnecessary surgical and diagnostic interventions. The inclusion of the terms “acute” and “chronic” in the classification of dynamic-pressure hydrocephalic conditions provides a more comprehensive description of the clinical presentation and may help to ensure that alternative treatment options are used earlier. The determination of the point at which chronicity becomes evident should be made on an individual basis, as the progression of this condition is influenced by various factors, the specific contribution of which is not always readily discernible. The presented case suggests that catheter-associated infection and subsequent ventriculitis might be a contributing factor. Other authors have suggested an association of PVL as well as inflammatory and degenerative changes that alter periventricular cerebral permeability.8–10

In the presented case, alterations in the subarachnoid septa were found during ETV, most likely due to inflammatory processes. Whether chronicity manifests as a result of these conditions remains unclear. More cases need to be evaluated and compared to strengthen this theory.

sec.title: Observations
sec.p: In this case, iSRP was found to be an effective method for stabilizing ventricle size without the need for further external ventricular drainage, which carries a risk of infection. The patient achieved a good clinical status with full alertness and orientation as well as complex speech production, so that she could finally be discharged home. Long-term follow-up will show whether fewer daily reservoir depressions are sufficient to maintain the clinical condition and ventricle size over time.

It is important to note that this approach should only be considered if standard subatmospheric treatment has failed. Without sufficient patient and/or care provider compliance, this approach is likely to fail. Short intervals between outpatient visits are recommended in order to detect any further complications at an early stage.

sec.title: Lessons
sec.p: Since VPS dysfunction in LPH or NegPH can be mistaken as a cause of persistent ventriculomegaly and poor clinical status, it is important to consider these rare manifestations early to prevent unnecessary interventions and treatment complications and to finally improve the patients’ outcomes. If standard therapy fails, chronicity must be assumed at an early stage, and alternative treatment options such as active iSRP must be initiated. The therapeutic goal is to improve the clinical condition of the patient and to provide outpatient care as soon as possible, as the treatment is already associated with a long hospital stay.
